name: Heartland Group Holdings Limited
overview: Heartland Group Holdings is a New Zealand/Australia-listed (NZX/ASX: HGH) specialist bank holding company, owning Heartland Bank Limited (NZ, registered bank since 2012) and Heartland Bank Australia Limited (an APRA-regulated ADI, acquired April 2024 from the former Challenger Bank/StockCo/Reverse Mortgages businesses). The group's core products are Reverse Mortgages (NZ and Australia, its dominant growth engine), Motor Finance, Rural/Livestock Finance, Business Finance, and Savings & Deposits, funded predominantly by retail deposits. On 2 June 2026 Heartland announced a conditional NZ$620m agreement to acquire TSB Bank from the Toi Foundation and merge it with Heartland Bank to form 'TSB Heartland Bank,' New Zealand's seventh-largest bank with ~NZ$15bn of assets, expected to complete December 2026.

business_model.summary: Heartland earns net interest margin on specialist niche lending books funded mainly by retail term deposits/on-call savings plus some wholesale/securitisation funding, supplemented by other operating income (fees, insurance). It deliberately avoids commoditised mainstream banking (e.g. standard home loans, credit cards) in favour of specialist niches where it can price for risk and service complexity that the major trans-Tasman banks largely ignore. FY2025 was a reset year: NPAT collapsed to $38.8m (underlying $46.9m) on elevated impairments and cost growth from the Australian ADI integration; 1H2026 shows a sharp recovery (reported NPAT $48.8m, underlying $46.1m) driven by NIM expansion, falling impairments, cost discipline and accelerated run-off of a non-strategic asset (NSA) portfolio.

revenue_streams.name: Reverse Mortgages (NZ + Australia)
revenue_streams.trend: growing strongly - NZ Receivables +15.2% annualised 1H2026, AU +18.9% annualised; the primary growth engine

revenue_streams.name: Motor Finance (NZ)
revenue_streams.trend: declining - deliberate strategic repositioning toward higher-quality franchise/direct channels; FY2026 guidance flat to -3%

revenue_streams.name: Rural / Livestock Finance (NZ + AU)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - NZ >9% FY2026 guided growth, AU Livestock Finance returned to growth in FY2025 after FY2024 decline

revenue_streams.name: Business Finance / Asset Finance (NZ)
revenue_streams.trend: declining sharply - down 22.8% annualised 1H2026, FY2026 guidance retraction of up to 19% on disciplined pricing/risk

revenue_streams.name: Non-Strategic Assets (NSA run-off)
revenue_streams.trend: shrinking to near zero - total NSA balance down from $364.8m (Jun-25) to $175.0m (Dec-25), tracking to be largely complete by 30 June 2026, recovery rate >90%

revenue_streams.name: Savings & Deposits / Net Interest Margin
revenue_streams.trend: core funding base - $6.53bn retail deposits (NZ $4.36bn, AU $2.17bn) supporting NIM of 3.92% in 1H2026, up 51bps YoY

business_model.customer_type: Predominantly B2C retail lending (reverse mortgage customers typically 60+ years old; motor finance consumers) plus B2B/agri (Rural and Livestock Finance to farmers, Business/Asset Finance to SMEs); deposit funding sourced from NZ and Australian retail savers.
business_model.geographic_mix: NZ Banking ~65% of group receivables ($4.46bn of $7.31bn at Dec-25), Australia ~34% (A$2.46bn); group reports in NZD with AU segment translated from AUD, creating FX sensitivity to the AUD/NZD cross rate.

main_competitors: Big four Australasian banks (ANZ, ASB/CBA, BNZ/NAB, Westpac) - dominant in mainstream deposits/mortgages but largely absent from reverse mortgages and thin-margin specialist niches
Bluestone / Household Capital / other Australian reverse mortgage and equity-release lenders
Resimac, Latitude, and other NZ/AU non-bank consumer and motor finance lenders
Rabobank and other agri-focused lenders in Rural/Livestock Finance
TSB Bank (pending merger target rather than competitor from Dec-2026)
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant niche leader: ~92% share of the New Zealand reverse mortgage market and ~40% share of the Australian reverse mortgage market (up from 36% a year earlier). A minor player in overall NZ/AU banking system assets (Heartland Bank's balance sheet is a small fraction of the majors'), but the clear specialist leader in its chosen product set.

moat_factors.factor: Reverse mortgage scale and origination network
moat_factors.description: Decade-plus head start, ~2,700 accredited Australian brokers, exclusive/preferred distribution relationships, and underwriting/servicing expertise in a complex, long-duration product that mainstream banks have chosen not to compete in due to duration mismatch, valuation/actuarial complexity and reputational sensitivity around elderly customers

Dual bank registration (RBNZ deposit-taker licence + APRA ADI licence) is costly and slow to obtain, deterring new entrants; existing registered-bank status also lets Heartland access cheaper retail deposit funding than non-bank finance companies
Specialist knowledge in livestock/rural finance (StockCo) and non-standard motor/asset finance that generalist banks are not set up to service profitably at Heartland's price points
Canstar NZ 'Savings Bank of the Year' for eight consecutive years; NZ Depositor Compensation Scheme (from 1 July 2025) narrows the safety perception gap with the majors for a small registered bank

Heartland is sub-scale versus the majors on a group-wide cost-to-income basis (54.6% underlying 1H2026 vs high-40s/low-50s at the majors); the TSB merger is explicitly aimed at fixing this via scale and funding-cost synergies

weaknesses: Small absolute scale versus the big four banks limits funding cost advantages and requires continuous wholesale/deposit competition for growth capital

Concentrated reliance on a single growth product (Reverse Mortgages) for the medium-term growth story while three of five core NZ product lines (Motor Finance, Business Finance, and previously NSAs) are shrinking or being wound down
History of credit-quality missteps in Motor Finance and Business Finance that required a costly FY2025 'reset,' raising questions about underwriting discipline through the cycle

Integration risk now doubled: Heartland Bank Australia integration (2024) is not yet fully bedded down (multi-year technology programme to FY2028) at the same time as the newly announced TSB Bank merger (targeted completion December 2026) is layered on top
ROE has been persistently below levels needed to justify a premium to book value; FY2026 guidance of ROE ≥7% is itself below most observers' estimate of Heartland's cost of equity

growth_drivers: Reverse Mortgage growth in both countries: NZ Receivables guided >18% FY2026 growth against a ~$170bn NZ TAM (currently $1.33bn drawn, ~92% market share); Australia against an estimated AU$600-660bn TAM (currently A$2.17bn drawn, ~40% share) - both markets structurally underpenetrated and supported by ageing demographics

TSB Bank merger (announced 2 June 2026, ~NZ$620m, expected completion December 2026): creates 'TSB Heartland Bank,' NZ's seventh-largest bank (~NZ$15bn total assets), management guiding to NZ$34m of annual run-rate synergies and >20% EPS accretion in year one - the single largest catalyst/re-rating event on the horizon

RBNZ capital settings review (final decisions 17 December 2025): reduced Tier 1 (14%→11%) and total capital (16%→14%) ratio requirements, removal of AT1 instruments, more granular/lower risk weights, and reduction of Heartland Bank's transitional capital overlay from 2.0% to 0.5% (effective 1 March 2026) - frees up an estimated ~$125-190m of excess regulatory capital for growth, buybacks or dividends
NSA realisation nearly complete (largely done by 30 June 2026) at a >90% recovery rate, releasing capital for redeployment into higher-ROE core lending and removing a persistent earnings drag

Technology programmes (~$17m over three years combined, ~$11m for Heartland Bank's Pega-based platform, plus a separate Australian platform consolidation) intended to unify origination/servicing, improve automation, and lower the cost-to-income ratio over the medium term
NZ Depositor Compensation Scheme (effective 1 July 2025) narrows the perceived safety gap between Heartland Bank and the major banks, supporting further growth in the low-cost retail deposit base

Management's FY2030 long-term ambition (to be detailed at an investor day, originally flagged for 5 June 2026) targeting materially higher underlying ROE and NPAT via capital efficiency, AU profit retention to fund growth, and CTI ratio reduction

business.risk: Motor Finance and Business Finance asset quality
business.description: FY2025 impairment expense rose 54.3% ($25.2m) on deteriorating NZ economic conditions; while 1H2026 shows sharp improvement (impairment expense ratio down to 0.35% from 1.40%), the core-portfolio NPL ratio was still 2.07% at Dec-2025 and Business Finance NPLs remain elevated (8.3% of the portfolio at Jun-25) in construction/transport/hospitality sectors

With Motor Finance and Business Finance both shrinking and NSAs nearly gone, medium-term growth is increasingly dependent on a single product line; any slowdown in reverse mortgage demand, house prices, or a competitive share loss (AU share already ceded ground briefly before recovering to 40%) would disproportionately hit growth

Large, complex bank-to-bank merger (creating a $15bn-asset combined entity) still conditional on Toi Foundation trustee approval (8 of 10 required), community consultation in Taranaki, RBNZ/FMA/APRA regulatory approval, and a Fitch rating confirmation (≥BBB stable); integration risk compounds an Australian ADI integration that is itself not yet complete

financial.description: NZ$210m equity raise in April 2024 to fund the Australian ADI acquisition; the TSB transaction adds a further ~$250m of new equity (200m shares at $1.25) plus $56m subordinated debt plus a $264m vendor loan from the Toi Foundation - cumulative dilution and leverage from two large deals within three years

Australian banking segment (~34% of group receivables) is reported in AUD and translated to NZD, creating earnings and receivables volatility from FX moves (1H2026 growth figures explicitly note FX impacts)

financial.risk: Wholesale/vendor funding reliance for TSB deal
financial.description: The TSB acquisition funding structure includes a $264m vendor loan from Toi Foundation and $56m of subordinated (Tier 2) debt, adding financial complexity and refinancing risk around completion

regulatory.description: Owning both an RBNZ-registered NZ bank and an APRA-regulated Australian ADI requires maintaining separate capital, risk and compliance infrastructure in each jurisdiction, adding structural cost (explicitly cited as a driver of FY2025 OPEX growth) and complexity that a single-country peer would not bear

RBNZ has indicated it will review reverse mortgage risk weights in 2026 following a 2023 adjustment; given reverse mortgages are Heartland's core growth product, an adverse risk-weight change would directly affect required capital and profitability of the core growth engine

regulatory.risk: Deposit Takers Act 2023 / Group Supervision Policy
regulatory.description: A formal RBNZ Group Supervision Policy for deposit takers is not expected until 1 December 2028; until then Heartland Bank retains a residual transitional capital overlay (reduced to 0.5% from 1 March 2026) with some regulatory uncertainty until the policy is finalised

macro.description: Reverse mortgage credit risk is primarily house-price-driven via the no-negative-equity guarantee; a sustained house price decline in NZ or Australia would increase future loss provisioning even though current weighted-average LVRs are conservative (27.1% NZ, 24.6% AU per FY2025 disclosure)

macro.risk: NZ/AU credit cycle and interest rate environment
macro.description: Motor Finance, Business Finance and Rural portfolios are exposed to consumer and SME credit stress; OCR trajectory affects both funding costs and loan demand - management notes pricing competition is expected to continue even as the OCR stabilises

macro.risk: Deposit competition against the big four
macro.description: As a small bank funding via retail deposits, Heartland must consistently offer above-market deposit rates to compete for funding against much larger, better-capitalised major banks, structurally pressuring net interest margin

execution.description: Founding CEO Jeff Greenslade retired after 15 years (30 September 2024), succeeded by long-tenured internal CFO/Head of Corporate Finance Andrew Dixson - continuity risk is mitigated by his 14-year internal tenure, but he is now the first non-founder CEO steering both the AU integration and the TSB merger simultaneously

Heartland is simultaneously running: (1) Australian bank integration/technology build to FY2028, (2) a ~$17m NZ+AU technology transformation, (3) NSA wind-down, and (4) the TSB Bank merger targeted for December 2026 completion - significant execution risk from overlapping, resource-intensive change initiatives

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ and Australian reverse mortgage markets are structurally under-penetrated (estimated combined TAM of NZ$170bn + AU$600-660bn against combined current Receivables of roughly NZ$1.33bn + AU$2.17bn) and are expected to grow with ageing populations - Heartland forecasts NZ 65+ population share rising from 17% (2024) to 21-24% by 2051, and Australian 65+ share rising to ~20% by 2066. Mainstream banking growth in NZ/AU is more mature and cyclically exposed to the credit cycle.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - Motor Finance, Business Finance and Rural/Livestock Finance are cyclical and were the source of FY2025's asset-quality reset; Reverse Mortgages are comparatively acyclical (demand driven by demographics and cost-of-living pressure on retirees rather than the broader credit cycle), providing some earnings ballast.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-high - NIM is directly sensitive to OCR moves and the shape of the funding curve; 1H2026 NIM expansion (+51bps to 3.92%) was driven by falling cost of funds, and management flags continued competitive deposit pricing pressure even as the OCR stabilises. Reverse mortgage accrual economics also embed an interest-rate assumption in fair-value measurement.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: AUD/NZD - roughly one-third of group receivables and earnings originate in Australia and are translated into NZD reporting currency.
key_input_costs: Broker/intermediary commissions (reverse mortgage and motor finance origination)

recent_developments.event: Announced conditional merger implementation agreement to acquire TSB Bank Limited from Toi Foundation Holdings for ~NZ$620m, creating 'TSB Heartland Bank' (NZ's 7th-largest bank, ~NZ$15bn total assets); funded via ~$250m new equity (200m shares at $1.25), $56m subordinated debt, and a $264m vendor loan from Toi Foundation; management guides to $34m annual synergies and >20% EPS accretion in year one; expected completion December 2026, subject to Toi Foundation trustee approval, Taranaki community consultation, and RBNZ/FMA/APRA regulatory approval plus a Fitch rating confirmation of at least BBB stable

1H2026 interim result: reported NPAT $48.8m (vs $3.6m 1H2025), underlying NPAT $46.1m (vs $10.7m); underlying ROE 7.3% (up 540bps); NIM 3.92% (up 51bps); underlying CTI ratio 54.6% (down 304bps); impairment expense down 74.7% to $12.8m; interim dividend declared 3.5cps (up from 2.0cps), payout ratio 72% (above the ≥50% policy floor); FY2026 guidance reaffirmed at underlying NPAT ≥$85m and underlying ROE ≥7%

RBNZ announced final decisions on deposit-taker capital settings: reduced Tier 1 (14%→11%) and total capital (16%→14%) requirements, removed AT1 instruments, more granular/lower risk weights; Heartland Bank's transitional capital overlay cut from 2.0% to 0.5% effective 1 March 2026 - releasing an estimated $125-190m of excess regulatory capital

FY2025 full-year result: reported NPAT $38.8m (down from $74.5m FY2024), underlying NPAT $46.9m (met ≥$45m guidance); NIM restored to 3.56% (+17bps); OPEX up 38.1% on ADI integration costs; impairment expense up 54.3% ($25.2m) on NZ credit deterioration in Motor Finance/Business Finance; final dividend 2.0cps, total FY2025 dividend 4.0cps (payout ratio 80%); FY2026 guidance issued (underlying ROE ≥7%, underlying NPAT ≥$85m)

Andrew Dixson (internal, ex-Group CFO) formally began as CEO succeeding founding CEO Jeff Greenslade, who retired after 15 years on 30 September 2024, following board/leadership changes through FY2025 including a new Chief Asset Management Officer, Chief Strategy Officer and Chief Digital Transformation Officer appointments
New Zealand Depositor Compensation Scheme came into effect, seen by management as a competitive opportunity for Heartland Bank to grow its share of domestic retail deposits

FY2026 full-year results announcement date set for 20 August 2026 - not yet released as of this analysis (11 August 2026); investors should treat guidance figures in this report as the latest confirmed target pending that release

guidance.as_of: 1H2026 Interim Results (25 February 2026), reaffirming FY2025 result guidance issued 21 August 2025

items.notes: Reaffirmed at 1H2026; split as NZ Banking >$45m and AU Banking >AU$37m (NZ$40m); 1H2026 underlying NPAT of $46.1m is already >54% of the full-year floor
Split as NZ Banking >6%, AU Banking >8%; 1H2026 underlying ROE was 7.3%, already above the full-year floor, though 2H typically softer historically

NZ Banking >4.10% (revised down 10bps from prior outlook due to Reverse Mortgage repricing and NSA realisation mix effects), AU Banking >3.70% (revised up 30bps on stronger deposit-led funding transition)

items.vs_prior: revised - NZ down $2.1m, AU up A$3.4m
items.notes: NZ Banking <$127m (lower than prior outlook), AU Banking <A$58m (higher, reflecting technology and marketing investment)

NZ Banking <56% (+250bps) reflecting subdued core lending growth and NSA-realisation revenue drag; AU Banking <50% (+450bps, i.e. guidance loosened despite improving trend, as AU absorbs technology and growth-related costs)
NZ Banking <0.70% (-15bps improvement); AU Banking <0.10% (unchanged, already very low)
Supported by a new marketing campaign live in 2H2026 (Judy Bailey brand ambassador) and strong new-business volumes (+23% YoY in 1H2026)
Receivables contraction in 1H2026 due to strategic shift to higher-quality channels
Deliberate disciplined pricing/risk approach amid subdued demand in transport and construction sectors

items.target: ≤$17m combined over 3 years (≤$11m Heartland Bank NZ Pega platform + Australian platform consolidation)
items.notes: AU technology full migration targeted for FY2028; NZ implementation phased Reverse Mortgages (FY2026) then Motor Finance/Savings & Deposits (FY2027) then Rural/Asset Finance/Collections (FY2028)
1H2026 interim dividend 3.5cps represented a 72% payout ratio, above the policy floor, reflecting the turnaround and excess capital position; DRP applies to the final dividend with no discount

items.target: NZ$34m annual run-rate synergies; >20% EPS accretion in year one
items.notes: Subject to deal completion; not yet reflected in FY2026 guidance figures above, which pre-date the TSB announcement

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Andrew Dixson (1H2026): 'Heartland delivered a strong turnaround in profitability and steady progress towards its FY2026 guidance, supported by NIM expansion, improved asset quality metrics, strong Reverse Mortgage growth in both countries, cost control and accelerated NSA realisation.' Management explicitly reaffirmed FY2026 guidance (underlying ROE ≥7%, underlying NPAT ≥$85m) at the 1H2026 result and flagged an investor day (originally slated for 5 June 2026) to present FY2030 long-term ambitions, though this now sits alongside the subsequently announced TSB Bank merger. Management has been explicit that ROE is now the group's 'key performance metric' following the FY2025 reset, and that historical low-teens ROE ambitions were rebased lower by the FY2025 reset before the current recovery trajectory.

bull_case: Sharp, quantified earnings turnaround already in train: underlying NPAT roughly quadrupled from $10.7m (1H2025) to $46.1m (1H2026) and underlying ROE rose 540bps to 7.3%, with 1H2026 already delivering >54% of the full-year ≥$85m NPAT guidance floor - the FY2025 'reset' appears to have bottomed

Dominant, hard-to-replicate niche moat in Reverse Mortgages (92% NZ market share, 40% AU share and rising) against a combined addressable market of roughly NZ$170bn + AU$600-660bn versus ~NZ$3.5bn currently drawn - a multi-decade demographic growth runway that mainstream banks structurally avoid

TSB Bank merger (announced June 2026, ~$620m) is a transformative scale event: creates NZ's seventh-largest bank (~$15bn assets), management guides to $34m of annual synergies and >20% year-one EPS accretion, directly addressing Heartland's key structural weakness (sub-scale cost base and elevated CTI ratio)

Regulatory tailwind from December 2025 RBNZ capital decisions: lower Tier 1/total capital requirements and a cut transitional overlay (2.0%→0.5%) free an estimated $125-190m of excess capital for growth, buybacks or dividends, while the NSA portfolio (down from $364.8m to $175.0m in just six months, >90% recovery rate) is nearly fully run off

Trading near or modestly above book value (P/B roughly 0.9-1.0x per recent data) gives meaningful re-rating potential if underlying ROE genuinely trends toward or above a ~9-10% cost of equity as guided improvements in NIM, CTI and impairments compound through FY2026-FY2028
bear_case: ROE has been structurally below a reasonable cost of equity for a specialist/higher-risk lender: FY2025 underlying ROE was just 4.2% (reported 3.2%) against a historical low-teens ambition, and even the FY2026 guidance floor of ≥7% would likely sit below Heartland's true cost of equity (typically estimated at 9-11%+ for a small dual-country bank) - meaning the stock may be a value trap rather than a re-rating story until ROE durably clears that hurdle

Execution risk is stacked three deep simultaneously: the Australian ADI integration (technology build not complete until FY2028), a ~$17m NZ/AU technology transformation just getting underway, and now the TSB Bank merger (targeted December 2026 completion, still conditional on trustee/community/regulatory approvals) - any one slipping would pressure the FY2026-FY2028 earnings trajectory

Growth is narrowing to a single product line: Motor Finance is guided flat-to-declining and Business Finance is guided to contract by up to 19% in FY2026 on deliberate de-risking, meaning medium-term growth depends almost entirely on Reverse Mortgages continuing to compound at >18%/year in both countries without a competitive or demand disruption

FY2025's credit-quality reset (impairment expense up 54.3% to a peak $50.5m in 1H2025, core-portfolio NPL still 2.07% at Dec-2025) demonstrates real underwriting weakness in Motor and Business Finance during a downturn - the 1H2026 recovery is encouraging but only two quarters of a durable trend, and NZ/AU credit and house-price cycles remain a live risk to reverse mortgage collateral values

Dilution and balance-sheet complexity from back-to-back capital raises: the $210m April 2024 raise for the Australian ADI and now a further ~$250m new equity plus $56m subordinated debt plus a $264m vendor loan for TSB materially increases share count and financial complexity within a three-year window, diluting per-share value creation even if the underlying business improves
